Renee of Ferrara
re-nā´ ŏv fĕ-rä´ra
n. (Renée of France, 1510–1575, daughter of Louis XII and duchess of Ferrara, who sheltered Calvin and the persecuted and held the Reformed faith against husband, son and Inquisition)
French Renée, from Latin renata, born again — a name her life made apt; Ferrara, the duchy of the Este in northern Italy.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Renée of Ferrara was married at twenty to Ercole d'Este and turned her court into a refuge. Calvin visited her in 1536 under the name Charles d'Espeville and corresponded with her for the rest of his life; Clement Marot, Vittoria Colonna and many lesser fugitives found shelter there. Her husband, under pressure from Rome and from his own political need, had her examined, separated her from her children, and in 1554 confined her until she made an outward submission. She did not change. Widowed in 1559 she returned to France, settled at Montargis, and opened it to Huguenot refugees after the massacres, refusing a royal order to surrender them and telling the commander that she would stand in the gate herself. Heb 13:2 was her practice — “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” — and Mat 25:35, “I was a stranger, and ye took me in.” Heb 11:25 names the choice she made at twenty and kept at sixty: “Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season.”

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines hospitality as the act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality.

HOSPITAL'ITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality.

REF'UGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress.

2. That which shelters or protects from danger, distress or calamity.

Key Scripture

Heb 13:2 — "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares."

Mat 25:35 — "For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:"

Heb 11:25 — "Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season;"

2Ti 1:16 — "The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus; for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain:"

Modern Corruption

Hospitality is treated now as a style of entertaining; in Renee's hands it was a capital offence, which is nearer the New Testament meaning.

expand to see more

The New Testament commands hospitality in a world where receiving the wrong guest could cost a household everything, and that is the setting of Heb 13:2 and of Paul's thanks for Onesiphorus, who “was not ashamed of my chain” (2Ti 1:16). Renée's Montargis was called the hotel of God by the refugees who reached it, and she kept it open against a royal command. The modern domestication of the word — hospitality as a gift for hosting — empties it of the risk that gave it meaning. Mat 25:35 puts the stranger taken in among the deeds the King will own at the judgment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the duty of shelter, and Renée's life also answers a narrower error. She was pressed for decades by husband, son, confessors and inquisitors, made one forced outward submission under confinement, and went straight back to the faith when she was free — which is why Calvin, who rebuked her freely on other matters, never doubted her. Heb 11:25 describes a choice made once and then made again every year for fifty-five years, and that is what perseverance looks like from inside a life.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek philoxenia (G5381), love of strangers, hospitality; xenos (G3581), a stranger; sugkakoucheomai (G4778), to suffer affliction with.

Greek philoxenia (G5381) — hospitality, love of strangers; Hebrews 13:2.

Greek xenos (G3581) — a stranger, a foreigner; Matthew 25:35.

Greek sugkakoucheomai (G4778) — to suffer hardship along with; Hebrews 11:25.

Usage

"“Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2) — her practice at Montargis."

"“I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Mat 25:35) — owned at the judgment."

"“Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God” (Heb 11:25) — her choice, kept fifty-five years."
